newsitem.title: USA: U.S. deficit reduction compromise likely-Stiglitz.
newsitem.headline: U.S. deficit reduction compromise likely-Stiglitz.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and Congress are likely to come to a compromise on deficit reduction in the near future but in the interim, fiscal policy is stalled, the chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers said on Monday.
"Fiscal policy is treading water with no further reduction in the deficit in all likelihood in 1997," Joseph Stiglitz said during the Chicago Board of Trade's annual economic outlook press briefing.
During his speech, Stiglitz hailed Clinton -- who appointed him chairman in June of 1995 -- as the first American president this century to reduce the U.S. deficit four years in a row.
"This administration has plans to eliminate the deficit in the next six years. Congress has another plan," Stiglitz told reporters.
"There is likely to be a compromise to this plan (that will) come into law in the near future," he said.
Before his speech, Stiglitz told Reuters that the White House's commitment to deficit reduction was creating an economic climate "in which the market will likely see lower interest rates."
During his speech, Stiglitz also said he believes a balanced budget agreement is more likely now that the U.S federal elections are over.
"I think we have an environment, and I think will make real progress towards reducing the deficit to zero by the year 2002," he said.
